title: Calcutta High Court quashes Ritabrata Banerjee's recognition as Leader of the Opposition
dek: Justice Krishna Rao told the Speaker to decide afresh within 10 days and also set aside the rebel chief whip's appointment; Banerjee says he will return with a majority of MLAs.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Calcutta High Court on Friday set aside the West Bengal Assembly Speaker's decision to recognise Ritabrata Banerjee, leader of the breakaway Trinamool Congress faction, as Leader of the Opposition, and told the Speaker to decide the question afresh within 10 days.

Justice Krishna Rao also set aside the appointment of Akhruzzaman, another rebel MLA, as the opposition's chief whip. The ruling, on a writ petition by Sovandeb Chattopadhyay of the Mamata Banerjee-led faction, is a setback for the rebel Democratic Trinamool Congress, which says it has the support of most of the party's MLAs. The court's detailed order had not been published by Friday evening, and the court's reasons were not yet known.

## What the court decided

The judge held that the Speaker's decision of 3 June was not sustainable in law and directed the Speaker, Rathindra Bose, to reconsider both appointments and pass a fresh, reasoned order "in accordance with the law" within 10 days, according to reports from the courtroom. The case is Sovandeb Chattopadhyay v. Speaker, West Bengal Legislative Assembly (WPO 276 of 2026). Judgment had been reserved on 21 November.

Mr Chattopadhyay's petition argued that the Speaker had ignored the party's own choice. According to reports of the hearings, about 70 party leaders, including Mr Banerjee, met at the Trinamool headquarters on 6 May and named Mr Chattopadhyay as Leader of the Opposition, and a signed resolution was sent to the Speaker on 19 May. His counsel, senior advocate Kalyan Bandopadhyay, questioned the Speaker's impartiality and argued that the Speaker had delayed the decision until the rebels broke away. He also argued that Article 212 of the Constitution, which bars courts from questioning Assembly proceedings on grounds of irregular procedure, should not shield the decision.

Mr Banerjee's counsel, senior advocate Jaydip Kar, argued that the question depended on the Election Commission, which is still deciding which faction is the real Trinamool, and that no law sets out how a Speaker must choose a Leader of the Opposition, so the choice could not be challenged. Counsel for the Speaker relied on the party-wide meeting and argued that the post could not be decided before the Speaker took office. The judge rejected the argument that the matter was pending before the Election Commission, noting that the party had not split on the day the Speaker announced his decision, according to one report.

## What they are saying

Mr Banerjee called the ruling "nothing unusual" and said the matter had simply gone back to the Speaker. "Let's wait for 10 days. We will be presenting ourselves to the Speaker," he said, adding that he would go with "the majority of the MLAs in our support", according to reports. He also mocked Trinamool MP Kalyan Banerjee, saying his criticism came from frustration at being unable to vote on the delimitation bill because of his suspension from Parliament.

No statement from the Speaker's office or from Mamata Banerjee had been reported by Friday evening, and it was not known whether either side would appeal to a division bench.

## Background

The Trinamool Congress lost the Assembly election to the BJP in May, ending 15 years in power, and became the main opposition party. Soon afterwards a group of its MLAs broke away under Mr Banerjee, who won the Uluberia Purba seat in Howrah district; Akhruzzaman represents Raghunathganj in Murshidabad. Reports differ on the size of the group: one said the rebels claimed 58 of the party's 80 MLAs, another said Mr Banerjee broke away with 59 others.

The Speaker recognised Mr Banerjee as Leader of the Opposition on 3 June. On 18 June Justice Rao refused to stay that decision, finding no prima facie illegality, and on 18 August a division bench let Mr Banerjee continue in the post on an interim basis while the single judge decided the petition. The Supreme Court earlier this month asked the High Court to deal quickly with a separate Trinamool plea seeking the disqualification of 10 rebel MLAs, including Mr Banerjee, under the anti-defection law; the Speaker has not ruled on those petitions.

In September the Election Commission gave the two sides temporary names while it decides who owns the party's name and twin-flower symbol: the Mamata All India Trinamool Congress and the Democratic Trinamool Congress. Both have since filed truckloads of affidavits, and each accuses the other of forgery.

## What happens next

The Speaker has until about 7 December to issue a fresh decision. The rebels say they will show him a majority of MLAs; the Mamata Banerjee faction is expected to press its May resolution. Either side can appeal Friday's ruling. The Election Commission's decision on the party's name and symbol, and the disqualification petitions, are still pending.
